Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- In keeping with President Obama's pledge of an administration that is "transparent and accountable," the White House has launched a site that promises to show taxpayers where their stimulus-package dollars are being spent. Visitors to Recovery.gov are greeted with a video message from President Obama. The site, Recovery.gov, allows visitors to track efforts to jump-start a teetering economy in the midst of a slumping housing market and massive job losses. It breaks down the $787 billion package by category: $288 billion for tax relief, $59 billion for health care, and so on. The site promises that more detailed spending information will be posted once federal agencies decide how they are going to allocate the money.  Learn more about where the money is going » . Using graphs, charts and layman's terminology, the online portal is an example of how the tech-savvy Obama administration is taking its message to the American people. While running for president, Obama harnessed the Web's fundraising and social-networking capabilities to energize his grass-roots campaign. And the moment he was sworn in as the 44th president of the United States, administration officials unveiled a sleek interactive version of Whitehouse.gov, the official White House Web site. Recovery.gov, launched within hours of Obama's signing of the stimulus bill Tuesday, continues the theme of offering information in a user-friendly format. Visitors are greeted by a brief video address from Obama. "The American Recovery and Reinvestment Plan represents a strategic and significant investment in our country's future," the president explains. "The size and scale of this plan demand unprecedented efforts to root out waste, inefficiency and unnecessary spending. Recovery.gov will be the online portal for these efforts." The site will publish information on how the stimulus funds will be spent in a "timely, targeted and transparent manner," Obama said. Edward Glaeser, a professor of economics at Harvard University, said transparency has "been a watch word for good government types for years." "There is sense that taxpayers will feel a lot better about this if they actually know where their money is going," Glaeser said. "Better transparency makes evaluation much easier." Glaeser pointed out that the idea behind Recovery.gov is not entirely new. He noted that the Office of Management and Budget has for years had a site where citizens can learn the available cost-benefit information of several government programs. Clicking on "Where is Your Money Going" on the new site brings up a chart displaying key areas where the $787 billion will be distributed, including tax relief, energy, health care and infrastructure and science. Under "Accountability and Transparency," there is a statement that reads, "This is your money. You have a right to know where it's going and how it's being spent. Learn what steps we're taking to ensure you can track our progress every step of the way." Like other Obama online portals, the site encourages user interaction. The public is invited to share stories on how the Recovery Act is affecting them. Scrolling over a map of the United States reveals data on the number of jobs created and saved in each state. Those with some time on their hands can also read, in its entirety, the full text of the legislation.

counterfactuals.output:
# Obama administration launches Recovery.gov to track stimulus spending

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — The Obama administration has launched a new website aimed at helping taxpayers follow how the federal government spends money from the $787 billion economic stimulus package.

Recovery.gov went online as President Barack Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act into law. The site is intended to provide the public with information about where stimulus funds are going, which projects receive money and how many jobs are created or preserved.

“This is your money,” Obama said in announcing the transparency effort, promising that Americans would be able to track federal spending “down to the local level.”

The recovery package includes funding for infrastructure projects, education, health care, renewable energy and aid to cash-strapped state governments, as well as tax relief for individuals and businesses. The administration says the measure is designed to help pull the nation out of recession and save or create millions of jobs.

At launch, Recovery.gov offers an overview of the legislation, breakdowns of major spending categories and explanations of how federal agencies will distribute the money. More detailed information, including reports from agencies and funding recipients, is expected to be added as projects get underway.

Vice President Joe Biden has been assigned a leading role in overseeing implementation of the stimulus plan. The Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board, chaired by former federal prosecutor Earl Devaney, will monitor spending and investigate potential waste, fraud and abuse.

The website is a key part of Obama’s pledge to make government more open and accountable. But watchdog groups and lawmakers say its effectiveness will depend on how quickly information is posted, how detailed it is and whether the data are easy for taxpayers to understand.

Republican critics, many of whom opposed the stimulus bill, have questioned whether the government can spend such a large amount of money quickly without wasting taxpayer dollars. Administration officials say public reporting and independent oversight will help reduce that risk.

The site also invites visitors to review spending data and report suspected fraud or misuse of recovery funds.

As billions of dollars begin moving through federal agencies and state governments, Recovery.gov is expected to become the central public portal for tracking one of the largest economic intervention efforts in U.S. history.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the launch of Recovery.gov, including its transparency goals, interactive features, spending breakdowns, Obama’s video message, and comments from Harvard economist Edward Glaeser.
counterfactuals.output:
## Launch of Recovery.gov

The Obama administration launched **Recovery.gov on February 17, 2009**, the day President Barack Obama signed the **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act**. The site was intended to give the public a central place to follow the roughly **$787 billion economic-stimulus program** and to discourage waste, fraud and political favoritism.

### Transparency goals

Recovery.gov promised to show:

- How much recovery money had been authorized, awarded and paid out;
- Which federal agencies, states, communities and contractors received funds;
- What projects were financed and how many jobs they were expected to create or preserve;
- Reports from inspectors general and the new Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board; and
- Ways for citizens to report suspected fraud, waste or abuse.

At launch, much of the information consisted of **planned allocations and estimates**, because little money had yet been distributed. Officials said the site would become more detailed as agencies and grant recipients began filing reports.

### Interactive features

The initial site offered maps, charts and timelines that allowed users to explore expected spending and employment effects by state. Visitors could select a state to see its projected share of recovery funds and estimated jobs. It also included explanations of the legislation, agency links, frequently asked questions and an online mechanism for submitting concerns.

The administration envisioned later versions allowing people to drill down to individual grants, contracts and local projects.

### Spending breakdown

The original $787 billion package was displayed in broad categories:

| Category | Approximate amount |
|---|---:|
| Tax relief | **$288 billion** |
| State and local fiscal relief | **$144 billion** |
| Infrastructure and science | **$111 billion** |
| Protecting vulnerable Americans | **$81 billion** |
| Health care | **$59 billion** |
| Education and training | **$53 billion** |
| Energy | **$43 billion** |
| Other programs | **$8 billion** |

These figures described how the law was expected to allocate funds, rather than money already spent.

### Obama’s video message

In a video posted on the site, Obama framed Recovery.gov as a public-accountability tool. His central message was: **“This is your money. You have a right to know where it’s going and how it’s being spent.”** He said the administration intended to provide an unprecedented level of openness and invited citizens to use the site to hold the government accountable. He also acknowledged that the launch version was only a starting point and that more information would appear as spending began.

### Edward Glaeser’s reaction

Harvard economist **Edward Glaeser** welcomed the emphasis on openness, arguing that public access to spending information could help outsiders identify bad projects and make misuse of funds more difficult. At the same time, he cautioned that merely posting numbers would not be enough: useful oversight required detailed, accessible data and a way to judge results, not simply lists of appropriations. In effect, the site’s value would depend on whether citizens, journalists and researchers could connect spending to actual projects and economic outcomes.

Overall, Recovery.gov began as an ambitious transparency promise, but its launch version was principally a framework for future reporting rather than a real-time ledger of stimulus expenditures.

**Obama Turns to New Website to Track Stimulus Spending**

**WASHINGTON, Feb. 18, 2009** — President Barack Obama is using a new government website to show Americans where money from the $787 billion economic stimulus package is being spent, part of an effort to make the massive program more transparent and accountable.

The site, **Recovery.gov**, was unveiled as Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act into law Tuesday. It is intended to provide information about federal spending on roads, schools, energy projects, health care and other programs designed to create jobs and help pull the country out of recession.

“This is your money,” Obama said in announcing the initiative. “You have a right to know where it’s going and how it’s being spent.”

The website currently offers summaries of the recovery plan, breakdowns of spending by category and explanations of the law’s tax provisions. Administration officials say it will eventually include state-by-state data, maps of funded projects and reports from agencies and recipients showing how the money is being used.

Recovery.gov is also expected to list contracts and grants while allowing taxpayers to report suspected waste, fraud or abuse.

The administration says the site will be updated as federal departments distribute funds and state and local governments begin work on projects. Because much of the money has not yet been awarded, detailed information about individual recipients remains limited.

Oversight of the program will be led by the Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board, a panel created under the law to monitor spending and investigate possible misuse of funds.

Obama has pledged that the recovery program will be conducted with an unusual degree of openness. The website is a central part of that promise, giving the public a single place to follow the flow of federal dollars as the stimulus effort moves forward.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe Recovery.gov and how it reflects the Obama administration’s pledge to make government more transparent, accountable, technologically savvy, and accessible to the public.
counterfactuals.output:
**Recovery.gov** was a public website created in 2009 to track spending under the **American Recovery and Reinvestment Act**, the roughly $800 billion economic-stimulus law enacted during the financial crisis. Operated by the independent **Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board**, it reported where recovery funds went, which agencies and recipients received them, what projects they supported, and how many jobs recipients said were created or retained. The site also published audits and agency reports and allowed users to report suspected fraud, waste, or abuse.

It embodied several Obama administration priorities:

- **Transparency:** Spending information was placed online in searchable, downloadable formats rather than remaining only in agency reports.
- **Accountability:** Public disclosure, inspector-general oversight, recipient reporting, and fraud-reporting tools made it easier to scrutinize agencies, contractors, grant recipients, and local governments.
- **Technological sophistication:** Interactive maps, data visualizations, databases, and machine-readable data were used to explain a large federal program.
- **Public accessibility:** Citizens could look up projects by location and see how federal money was being used in their own communities.

Recovery.gov thus became an early flagship of the administration’s broader **open-government** agenda: using digital tools and public data to make federal spending more visible and officials more answerable. Its information was not perfect—recipient data could be delayed or contain errors, and job estimates were disputed—but the site established an influential model later applied to wider federal spending transparency. The Recovery Board and active site concluded their work in 2015, with records subsequently archived.

# White House launches online portal to track stimulus spending

**WASHINGTON —** The White House has launched an online portal designed to show Americans how money from the federal economic-stimulus package is being distributed, while giving the public tools to monitor projects, review state-level employment data and report suspected waste or fraud.

The website, **Recovery.gov**, was created after President Barack Obama signed the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009. The legislation authorized roughly $787 billion in tax cuts, aid to states and spending intended to create or preserve jobs during the recession.

Administration officials said the portal would be expanded as federal departments award grants, sign contracts and transfer funds to state and local governments. At launch, much of the site focused on explaining how the legislation divided the money rather than identifying individual recipients, because many awards had not yet been made.

## Spending divided into major categories

Recovery.gov organizes the package into broad policy areas, allowing visitors to see how much of the law is devoted to priorities such as:

- **Tax relief**, including credits and other provisions intended to increase household income and encourage business investment;
- **Health care**, including assistance for state Medicaid programs, health-information technology and medical research;
- **Education and training**, including aid to schools, support for students and workforce-development programs;
- **Infrastructure and science**, covering transportation projects, public facilities, broadband development and research;
- **Energy**, including renewable-power initiatives, energy-efficiency programs and improvements to the electric grid;
- **Protection for vulnerable Americans**, such as expanded food, housing and unemployment assistance; and
- **State and local fiscal relief**, intended to help governments maintain essential services and limit layoffs.

The site presents the categories through charts and summaries explaining the goals of each portion of the law. Tax relief represents one of the largest components, while direct spending is spread among agencies responsible for transportation, health, education, energy, housing and other programs.

## State-level jobs and economic data

A major feature of the portal is its state-by-state information. Users can select a state to review economic indicators, including unemployment figures and employment conditions.

The administration said the state pages would eventually provide more detailed information about projects, grants, contracts and the number of jobs reported as created or retained through stimulus funding.

Measuring employment effects, however, is more complicated than counting federal awards. Some projects can be linked to specific hiring, while tax provisions or aid that helps a state avoid layoffs may have a less direct effect. Early data on the site therefore provide a snapshot of local economic conditions rather than a complete accounting of stimulus-related jobs.

As agencies and funding recipients submit reports, the government plans to add geographic tools showing where money is being spent. The goal is to let residents move from a national overview to information about their state, community or congressional district.

## Public participation and oversight

Recovery.gov also invites the public to take part in monitoring the program. Visitors can submit comments, ask questions and share information about how the recession or stimulus initiatives are affecting their communities.

The portal includes links for reporting suspected fraud, waste or abuse. Those reports can be directed to inspectors general and other federal oversight officials charged with investigating the use of recovery funds.

That public role is central to the administration’s effort to present the stimulus as more transparent than previous large federal spending initiatives. The website is intended not only to promote the legislation but also to create a public record that journalists, watchdog groups, researchers and taxpayers can examine.

Oversight of the spending is led by the **Recovery Accountability and Transparency Board**, working with agency inspectors general and the Office of Management and Budget. Federal departments are also required to follow reporting standards for grants, loans and contracts funded through the recovery law.

## Agency allocations to be published

The White House said the portal would publish increasingly detailed information as agencies finalize their spending plans and allocate funds.

Those updates are expected to identify:

- Which federal agency received the money;
- Which program is responsible for distributing it;
- Whether the funding was issued as a grant, contract, loan or direct payment;
- The state or locality in which the money is being used;
- The recipient or contractor;
- The purpose and status of the project; and
- Employment results reported by recipients.

Agency-level data are particularly important because the stimulus law does not operate as a single federal program. Money flows through dozens of departments and offices, and in many cases passes through state governments before reaching schools, transportation authorities, health systems, businesses or nonprofit organizations.

The administration has said agencies will publish plans explaining how they intend to spend their shares of the package. As awards are made, Recovery.gov is expected to shift from a broad presentation of authorized funding to a searchable database of actual obligations and expenditures.

## Transparency will depend on the data

The portal represents an ambitious effort to give the public near-real-time access to information about one of the largest economic interventions in U.S. history. But its usefulness will depend on the accuracy, consistency and timeliness of reports submitted by agencies and recipients.

At the outset, the website offers more detail about what the stimulus law is intended to do than about where every dollar has gone. That is likely to change as projects begin, contracts are awarded and reporting deadlines take effect.

For the White House, the portal serves two purposes: making the case that the stimulus is addressing urgent economic needs and giving Americans a way to judge whether the money is being spent as promised.
